body:
The parent issue with description is #2690 

Proposed level changes for requirement in chapter "V12 File and Resources"

Full list of requirements for the chapter is listed here: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x20-V12-Files-Resources.md

| # | Description | Level change |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **1.12.3** | [ADDED] Verify that, if the application allows uploading files, the documentation defines the permitted file types, expected file extensions, and maximum size (including unpacked size) for each upload feature. Additionally, ensure that the documentation specifies how files are made safe for end-users to download and process. | 1 > 2 |
| **12.1.3** | Verify that a file size quota and maximum number of files per user is enforced to ensure that a single user cannot fill up the storage with too many files, or excessively large files. | 2 > 3 |
| **12.1.4** | [ADDED] Verify that the application does not allow uploading compressed files containing symlinks unless this is specifically required (in which case it will be necessary to enforce an allowlist of the files that can be symlinked to). | 2 > 3 |
| **12.1.5** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 12.2.1] Verify that when the application accepts a file, either on its own or within an archive such as a zip file, it checks if the file extension matches an expected file extension and validates that the contents correspond to the type represented by the extension. This includes, but is not limited to, checking the initial 'magic bytes', performing image re-writing, and using specialized libraries for file content validation. | 2 > 1 |
| **12.1.6** | [ADDED] Verify that the application blocks uploaded images with a pixel size larger than the maximum allowed, to prevent pixel flood attacks. | 1 > 3 |
| **12.4.4** | [ADDED] Verify that server-side file processing such as file decompression ignores user-provided path information to prevent vulnerabilities such as zip slip. | 1 > 3 |
| **12.5.3** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 12.3.4] Verify that the application validates or ignores user-submitted filenames, including in a JSON, JSONP, or URL parameter and specifies a filename in the Content-Disposition header field in the response. | 1 > 2 |
| **12.5.4** | [ADDED] Verify that file names served (e.g., in HTTP response header fields or email attachments) are encoded or sanitized (e.g., following RFC 6266) to preserve document structure and prevent injection attacks. | 1 > 2 |
| **12.5.5** | [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 12.4.2] Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are scanned by antivirus scanners to prevent serving of known malicious content. | 1 > 2 |
| **12.7.1** | [ADDED] Verify that the application proactively releases system resources, such as database connections, open files and threads when it finishes using them to prevent resource exhaustion. | 2 > 3 |

comments.body: I'm not sure about 12.1.5 being a L1 requirement.

> I'm not sure about 12.1.5 being a L1 requirement.

I politely think that file content validation is super important and worthy of L1.

As we had a similar discussion for input validation requirements, I agree that this "consideration" is easy to come by.

With input validation, including validating files, I think we need to use a bit of a different explanation than "you have a vulnerability in your application if the requirement is not satisfied" - it maybe does not provide so-called technical exploit, but the application does not provide validated input for business decisions and we need to watch it as an integrity problem. If you can not trust the input, it does not satisfy the need for your business process. "Usual" input validation is L1, so it is aligned with this.
I agree with your reasoning, Elar. I spent a lot of years specializing in building file upload security systems and the impact of these mistakes is yuge.

Current 11.3.1
> V11.3.1 Verify that input is validated to **enforce business or functional expectations for that input**. This should either use positive validation against an allowed list of values, patterns or ranges or alternatively be based on comparing to an expected structure or logical limit, according to pre-defined rules. For L1 this can focus on input which is used to make specific business or security decisions. **For L2 and up, this should apply to all input**.

To be fully aligned with 11.3.1, maybe we need to write some extra piece into 12.1.5 to say, that for files used for "enforce business or functional expectations" must be validated from L1, in general from L2?

My instinct is to drop the section "For L1 this can focus on input which is used to make specific business or security decisions. For L2 and up, this should apply to all input" and to shorten the requirement and make it L1. The split-level requirement really throws me off.

Most of these level choices are fairly subjective and will change based on the context of the app itself.

But if you wish to keep it in; I think doing the same for 12.1.5 is very reasonable.

I don't like this split requirement either, but I admit that all input validation and file uploads are not equally important, and if to make a list of "first priority tasks", then it gives some flexibility there to ignore not-that-important ones during the first wave. At the moment we don't have this flexibility in 12.1.5
I opened a separate issue for 12.1.5 content: #2733. One way or another, the level for 12.1.5 starts from L1. So I PR the  changes in.

I think this makes a lot of sense Elar.

And by the way, even though I’m not a fan of split level requirements, the more I dig into the current status of ASVS the more I run situations why I also think it needs to happen. 

So two thumbs up to the general direction.

And a lot of the level changes have taken things that traditionally were extremely important and caused me to reevaluate if they really are or not. I think you’re doing a very good job here. It’s just a relatively big change from the past which is why you saw some of my comments.

But when I look into your logic, I think you’re on the right path, sincerely.

@elarlang I was a bit surprised to see defense against zip slip as a level 3 requirement, I'm curious what your rationale was? I've seen more than one occasion where a simple zip slip attack was a direct pathway to RCE.

First, it is not me alone deciding those levels.

For zip slip situation to happen there are many preconditions that makes the likelihood a bit lower:

* It is allowed to upload zip (any archive) files
* AND it is processed (unpacked) on the server side
* AND file names from the container are used when storing files on the server side
* AND (
    * The library used does not have a defense against that
    * OR the code is custom-made
* )
* AND there must be follow-up vector available

I would say the level could be also 2, it is not always clear (and then other people ask, why it is level 2 :) ). It may require evaluation per application needs, [as stated in the document](https://asvs.dev/v5.0.0/What-is-the-ASVS/#level-evaluation)

> The rigorous discussions around both the criteria and the leveling decisions have resulted in an allocation which should hold true for the vast majority of cases, whilst accepting that it may not be a 100% fit for every situation. This means that in certain cases, organizations may wish to prioritize requirements from a higher level earlier on based on their own specific risk considerations.


In a way, you can watch zip slip also as a "path traversal requirement" that is level 1:

> 5.3.2	Verify that when the application creates file paths for file operations, instead of user-submitted filenames, it uses internally generated or trusted data, or if user-submitted filenames or file metadata must be used, strict validation and sanitization must be applied. This is to protect against path traversal, local or remote file inclusion (LFI, RFI), and server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks.
